learning_activity_name: Describe the concept of Chemistry (meaning, branches, applications and relationships with other disciplines)
sla_name: Meaning and Branches of Chemistry
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly define chemistry and list its main branches with examples of application.
sla_teaching_aids: Chart showing branches of chemistry|Textbook|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and changes that matter undergoes. It links closely with other sciences such as physics, biology and geology.
sla_notes_details: The major branches of chemistry include organic chemistry (compounds of carbon), inorganic chemistry (non-carbon compounds and elements), physical chemistry (energy and rates of reactions), analytical chemistry (identifying and measuring substances) and biochemistry (chemical processes in living things). Chemistry provides the scientific basis for medicine, agriculture, industry and environmental management.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, organic chemistry explains how sugar (C6H12O6) is broken down in the body, while inorganic chemistry explains the properties of table salt (NaCl).
sla_notes_daily_life: Chemistry knowledge is applied daily in cooking, cleaning, farming (fertilizers) and manufacturing of soap and medicine.
sla_exercise: What is chemistry?::Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter.||Name any three branches of chemistry.::Organic chemistry, inorganic chemistry and physical chemistry (also analytical chemistry and biochemistry).||State one relationship between chemistry and biology.::Biochemistry applies chemical principles to explain chemical processes occurring in living organisms.

sla_name: Chemistry and the Development of Society

sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/charts of industrial products|Samples of fertilizer, soap and medicine|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Chemistry has contributed enormously to the development of modern society through agriculture, medicine, industry and environmental protection.
sla_notes_details: In agriculture, chemistry enabled the production of fertilizers such as NPK that increase crop yields, and pesticides that protect crops. In medicine, chemistry underpins the manufacture of drugs such as antibiotics and painkillers. In industry, chemistry enabled production of plastics, soap and building materials, while in environmental management chemistry provides methods for treating water and controlling pollution.
sla_notes_illustrations: Chlorine gas is used to disinfect public water supplies, killing disease-causing micro-organisms and making water safe for drinking.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fertilizers manufactured through chemical processes help farmers increase food production for growing populations.
sla_exercise: Give one example of how chemistry has contributed to modern agriculture.::Chemistry enabled the manufacture of fertilizers such as NPK, which increase crop yields.||How does chemistry contribute to public health?::Chemistry enables the manufacture of medicines and disinfectants such as chlorine used to purify drinking water.||Name one industrial product that results from applied chemistry.::Plastics (polymers) or soap are products of applied chemistry.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concept of matter (physical and chemical changes of matter)
sla_name: Physical and Chemical Changes of Matter
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly distinguish physical from chemical changes using given examples.
sla_teaching_aids: Ice cubes|Candle|Magnesium ribbon|Beaker|Bunsen burner|Matchbox
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and it can exist as a solid, liquid or gas. Matter can undergo physical or chemical changes.
sla_notes_details: A physical change alters the form or state of matter without forming a new substance, for example melting of ice. A chemical change forms one or more new substances with different properties from the original, for example burning of magnesium ribbon in air, which produces magnesium oxide: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.
sla_notes_illustrations: Burning magnesium ribbon produces a bright white flame and leaves behind a white powder, magnesium oxide, which is a completely new substance different from the shiny grey metal.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cooking food, such as frying an egg, is a chemical change, while boiling water to make tea is only a physical change.
sla_exercise: Is melting of ice a physical or chemical change? Explain.::It is a physical change because no new substance is formed; only the state of water changes from solid to liquid.||Write the equation for burning magnesium ribbon in air.::2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO||Give one difference between a physical and a chemical change.::A physical change does not form a new substance and is usually reversible, while a chemical change forms a new substance and is usually irreversible.

sla_name: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly classify given substances as elements, compounds or mixtures and write correct chemical symbols.
sla_teaching_aids: Copper wire|Sulphur powder|Iron filings|Salt and water|Periodic table chart|Test tubes
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An element is a pure substance made of one type of atom and represented by a chemical symbol; a compound is formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio; a mixture is formed when two or more substances are combined physically without a fixed ratio.
sla_notes_details: Chemical symbols are assigned using the first letter (capitalized) of the element's English or Latin name, with a second lower-case letter added if needed to avoid confusion, for example Fe for iron (from Latin ferrum). A binary compound contains exactly two different elements, such as sodium chloride (NaCl). Mixtures can be homogeneous solutions, such as salt dissolved in water, or heterogeneous mixtures, such as sand and iron filings, and unlike compounds, the components of a mixture keep their individual properties and can be separated by physical methods.
sla_notes_illustrations: Iron filings mixed with sulphur powder form a mixture that can still be separated using a magnet, but heating them together forms the compound iron(II) sulphide: Fe + S -> FeS, which can no longer be separated by a magnet.
sla_notes_daily_life: Sea water is a natural mixture of water and dissolved salts, while the air we breathe is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
sla_exercise: What is a binary compound? Give an example.::A binary compound is a compound made up of two different elements chemically combined, for example sodium chloride, NaCl.||Write the equation for the formation of iron(II) sulphide from iron and sulphur.::Fe + S -> FeS||How can iron filings be separated from sulphur powder in a mixture?::By using a magnet, since iron is magnetic and sulphur is not.

sla_name: Properties of Compounds Compared to Their Elements
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly compare and explain the differences in properties between a compound and its constituent elements.
sla_teaching_aids: Iron filings|Sulphur powder|Test tube|Bunsen burner|Magnet|Dilute hydrochloric acid
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: When elements combine chemically to form a compound, the resulting compound has properties that are completely different from those of the individual elements that formed it.
sla_notes_details: Iron is a grey, magnetic metal, and sulphur is a yellow, non-magnetic non-metal; however, when heated together they form iron(II) sulphide (FeS), a dark solid that is neither magnetic nor yellow. This demonstrates that a compound is a genuinely new substance and cannot be separated back into its elements by simple physical methods such as using a magnet.
sla_notes_illustrations: Iron(II) sulphide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen sulphide gas, a reaction not shown by iron or sulphur alone: FeS + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2S.
sla_notes_daily_life: Rust, iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3), is reddish-brown and brittle, completely unlike the shiny, strong, grey iron metal it forms from.
sla_exercise: Is iron(II) sulphide magnetic like iron metal? Explain.::No, iron(II) sulphide is not magnetic because it is a new compound with different properties from its constituent element iron.||Write the equation for the reaction between iron(II) sulphide and dilute hydrochloric acid.::FeS + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2S||State one property of rust that differs from iron metal.::Rust (Fe2O3) is reddish-brown and brittle while iron metal is grey, shiny and malleable.

sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly locate given elements among the first 20 and classify each as a metal or non-metal.
sla_teaching_aids: Periodic table chart|Element cards|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number into rows called periods and columns called groups, with elements of similar properties placed in the same group.
sla_notes_details: The first 20 elements range from hydrogen (atomic number 1) to calcium (atomic number 20). Most of these elements are metals, which are generally good conductors of heat and electricity and are malleable, such as sodium, magnesium and calcium, while a smaller number are non-metals, such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine, which are poor conductors.
sla_notes_illustrations: Group I elements such as lithium, sodium and potassium are soft, reactive metals, while group VII (17) elements such as fluorine and chlorine are reactive non-metal gases.
sla_notes_daily_life: Aluminium, a metal, is used to make cooking pots because it conducts heat well, while oxygen, a non-metal gas, is essential for breathing and burning fuels.
sla_exercise: Name the first element in the periodic table and state whether it is a metal or non-metal.::Hydrogen is the first element; it is generally classified as a non-metal.||In which group are sodium, lithium and potassium found?::Group I (the alkali metals).||State one physical property common to metals.::Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity (also malleable and ductile).

sla_teaching_aids: Test tubes|Beakers|Conical flask|Bunsen burner|Fire extinguisher|First aid kit|Safety goggles|Laboratory coat
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A chemistry laboratory is a specially equipped room where experiments are carried out safely using proper apparatus and chemicals.
sla_notes_details: Important laboratory rules include wearing protective clothing such as a lab coat and safety goggles, avoiding eating or drinking in the laboratory, reporting spills immediately, and handling chemicals and open flames carefully. Learners must also know basic first aid measures for burns, cuts and chemical splashes, and the location and use of firefighting equipment such as fire extinguishers and fire blankets. Common apparatus include test tubes, beakers, conical flasks, burettes, pipettes and Bunsen burners, each used for a specific purpose.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Bunsen burner is used to heat substances directly with a controlled flame, while a beaker is used for mixing or holding liquids that do not need very precise measurement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Safety habits developed in the laboratory, such as careful handling of hot objects and chemicals, also protect people when handling cleaning agents or cooking at home.
sla_exercise: Name two pieces of protective clothing/equipment used in the chemistry laboratory.::Laboratory coat and safety goggles.||What should a learner do first if a chemical spills on the skin?::Wash the affected area immediately with plenty of clean water and inform the teacher.||Name one apparatus used to heat substances in the laboratory.::A Bunsen burner.

sla_name: Experiment: Changes of State of Matter
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly perform and record observations of melting, boiling, freezing and condensation.
sla_teaching_aids: Ice|Beaker|Thermometer|Bunsen burner|Tripod stand|Wire gauze|Stopwatch
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Matter changes from one physical state to another (solid, liquid or gas) when heated or cooled, without any new substance being formed.
sla_notes_details: Heating ice causes melting, changing it from solid to liquid at 0°C, and continued heating causes boiling, changing it from liquid to gas at 100°C for pure water; cooling water vapour causes condensation back to liquid, and cooling water causes freezing back to solid. These are physical changes because the chemical composition of water, H2O, remains the same throughout.
sla_notes_illustrations: A heating curve plotted for ice shows the temperature rising, then staying flat at 0°C while the ice melts, rising again, then staying flat at 100°C while the water boils, despite continuous heating.
sla_notes_daily_life: Formation of dew on grass in the early morning (condensation) and drying of wet clothes in the sun (evaporation) are everyday examples of changes of state.
sla_exercise: At what temperature does pure water boil at standard atmospheric pressure?::100 degrees Celsius (100°C).||What is the term for a liquid changing into a gas?::Boiling (or evaporation).||Why does the temperature stay constant while ice is melting, even though heating continues?::The heat energy is used to break the bonds holding the solid particles together (latent heat) rather than to raise the temperature.

sla_name: Experiment: Separating Mixtures
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly select and apply an appropriate method to separate a given mixture into its components.
sla_teaching_aids: Sand and water|Salt solution|Filter paper and funnel|Evaporating dish|Separating funnel|Magnet|Iron filings
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Mixtures are separated by methods that exploit differences in the physical properties of their components, such as particle size, solubility, density or magnetism.
sla_notes_details: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, such as sand from water; evaporation and crystallization recover a dissolved solid from a solution, such as salt from salt water; a separating funnel is used to separate two immiscible liquids, such as oil and water; and a magnet separates magnetic materials, such as iron filings, from non-magnetic materials such as sand.
sla_notes_illustrations: To obtain pure salt from salty water, the mixture is heated in an evaporating dish until the water evaporates completely, leaving behind solid sodium chloride (NaCl) crystals.
sla_notes_daily_life: Filtering muddy water through a clean cloth before drinking it, and using a sieve to remove stones from rice, are common household applications of separation techniques.
sla_exercise: Which method is used to separate sand from water?::Filtration.||Which method is used to recover salt from salt solution?::Evaporation (followed by crystallization).||Which apparatus is used to separate two immiscible liquids such as oil and water?::A separating funnel.

learning_activity_name: Describe the modern concept of atomic structure (Dalton's atomic structure and sub-atomic particles)
sla_name: Atomic Structure: Dalton's Theory and Sub-atomic Particles
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly state Dalton's postulates and identify the three sub-atomic particles with their charges.
sla_teaching_aids: Atomic structure model/chart|Manila paper|Marker pens|Textbook
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. Dalton's atomic theory proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms.
sla_notes_details: Modern experiments have shown that atoms are actually made up of three sub-atomic particles: protons, which carry a positive charge and are found in the nucleus; neutrons, which carry no charge and are also found in the nucleus; and electrons, which carry a negative charge and move around the nucleus. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, which is why the atom has no overall electric charge.
sla_notes_illustrations: A carbon atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons; the protons and neutrons are packed tightly in the small central nucleus, while the electrons move around it in shells.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding atomic structure underlies technologies such as X-ray imaging used in hospitals and smoke detectors that rely on radioactive elements.
sla_exercise: Name the three sub-atomic particles found in an atom.::Protons, neutrons and electrons.||State the charge of a proton, neutron and electron.::Proton is positive, neutron is neutral (no charge), electron is negative.||Where in the atom are protons and neutrons found?::In the nucleus, at the centre of the atom.

sla_teaching_aids: Periodic table chart|Bohr model diagrams|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Electrons in an atom are arranged in energy levels, called shells, around the nucleus, with a maximum number of electrons allowed in each shell.
sla_notes_details: The first shell can hold a maximum of 2 electrons, the second shell a maximum of 8, and the third shell up to 8 for the first 20 elements. Electrons fill the shell closest to the nucleus first before occupying the next one, and the arrangement is written as numbers separated by commas, for example sodium (atomic number 11) has the arrangement 2,8,1.
sla_notes_illustrations: Chlorine, atomic number 17, has the electronic arrangement 2,8,7, while calcium, atomic number 20, has the arrangement 2,8,8,2.
sla_notes_daily_life: The number of electrons in the outer shell largely determines how reactive an element is, which explains why sodium reacts vigorously with water while argon, a noble gas, does not react at all.
sla_exercise: What is the maximum number of electrons that the first shell can hold?::2 electrons.||Write the electronic arrangement of sodium (atomic number 11).::2,8,1||Write the electronic arrangement of chlorine (atomic number 17).::2,8,7

sla_name: Atomic Number and Mass Number
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly calculate the atomic number, mass number and number of neutrons for given elements.
sla_teaching_aids: Periodic table chart|Worked examples on manila paper|Calculators
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The atomic number (Z) of an element is the number of protons in its nucleus, while the mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
sla_notes_details: Since the number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom, the atomic number also tells us the number of electrons present. The number of neutrons is found by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number (neutrons = A - Z). Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, because they have different numbers of neutrons.
sla_notes_illustrations: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11, so it has 11 protons, 11 electrons, and 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons.
sla_notes_daily_life: Carbon-14, an isotope of carbon, is used by scientists to determine the age of ancient wooden artefacts and fossils through radiocarbon dating.
sla_exercise: Define atomic number.::The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.||An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?::12 neutrons (23 - 11 = 12).||What is an isotope?::An isotope is an atom of the same element with the same atomic number but a different mass number (different number of neutrons).

sla_notes_intro: Valence, or combining power, is the number of electrons an atom gains, loses or shares when forming compounds, and it determines the ratio in which elements combine.
sla_notes_details: Oxidation state indicates the apparent charge an atom has within a compound, while a radical is a group of atoms that behaves as a single charged unit, such as the sulphate radical, SO4^2-. In naming binary inorganic compounds, the metal (or less electronegative element) is named first, followed by the non-metal with its ending changed to '-ide'; where a metal has variable valence, its oxidation state is shown using Roman numerals in brackets.
sla_notes_illustrations: Iron(III) chloride, FeCl3, shows iron with an oxidation state of +3 combined with three chloride ions, while sodium and oxygen combine to form Na2O, named sodium oxide.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading and understanding the correct chemical name on a fertilizer or medicine label, such as calcium chloride (CaCl2), depends on knowing these nomenclature rules.
sla_exercise: What is valence?::Valence is the combining power of an atom, i.e. the number of electrons it gains, loses or shares in forming compounds.||Write the formula of iron(III) chloride.::FeCl3||Give the chemical formula of the sulphate radical.::SO4^2-

sla_name: Empirical and Molecular Formulae
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly determine the empirical and molecular formula of a compound from given data.
sla_teaching_aids: Calculators|Periodic table|Worked example charts|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound, while the molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule.
sla_notes_details: To find an empirical formula, the mass or percentage of each element is divided by its relative atomic mass to obtain mole values, and the resulting mole ratios are simplified to the smallest whole numbers. The molecular formula is then found as a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, once the relative molecular mass of the compound is known.
sla_notes_illustrations: Glucose has empirical formula CH2O, which has a formula mass of 30; since the relative molecular mass of glucose is 180, the multiple is 180 divided by 30, which is 6, giving the molecular formula C6H12O6.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of chemical formulae helps pharmacists and chemists accurately determine the exact composition of drugs and industrial chemicals.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between an empirical formula and a molecular formula?::The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound, while the molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.||The empirical formula of glucose is CH2O with formula mass 30. If its molar mass is 180, what is its molecular formula?::C6H12O6||A compound contains carbon and hydrogen only in the ratio CH2. Is this necessarily its molecular formula? Explain.::Not necessarily; CH2 is the empirical (simplest ratio) formula, and the actual molecular formula could be a whole-number multiple of it, such as C2H4.

sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly distinguish covalent bonding from electrovalent bonding using given examples.
sla_teaching_aids: Ball-and-stick molecular models|Periodic table|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Atoms bond together to achieve a stable electron arrangement, usually eight electrons in the outer shell, by either sharing or transferring electrons.
sla_notes_details: A covalent bond forms when two atoms, usually non-metals, share one or more pairs of electrons, as in water (H2O) or chlorine gas (Cl2). An electrovalent (ionic) bond forms when electrons are completely transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other, as in sodium chloride, NaCl, where sodium loses one electron to form Na+ and chlorine gains it to form Cl-.
sla_notes_illustrations: In sodium chloride, sodium's arrangement changes from 2,8,1 to 2,8 by losing one electron, and chlorine's arrangement changes from 2,8,7 to 2,8,8 by gaining that electron, forming Na+ and Cl- ions that attract each other.
sla_notes_daily_life: Table salt (NaCl) is an ionic compound that dissolves easily in water and conducts electricity when molten or dissolved, properties that make it useful in cooking and food preservation.
sla_exercise: What type of bond is formed by sharing of electrons between atoms?::A covalent bond.||What type of bond is formed by transfer of electrons between atoms?::An electrovalent (ionic) bond.||Describe the bond formed in sodium chloride, NaCl.::Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- ions which attract each other by an electrovalent (ionic) bond.

sla_notes_intro: A chemical equation is a shorthand way of representing a chemical reaction using the chemical formulae of the reactants and products.
sla_notes_details: A balanced equation has equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides, in line with the law of conservation of mass. The main types of chemical reactions include combination (two substances forming one product), decomposition (one substance breaking into two or more), displacement (one element replacing another in a compound), and neutralization (an acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water).
sla_notes_illustrations: Magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid is a displacement reaction: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, while heating calcium carbonate is a decomposition reaction: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
sla_notes_daily_life: Baking powder releasing carbon dioxide gas when heated inside a cake is an everyday decomposition-type reaction that makes cakes rise.
sla_exercise: Balance the equation: Mg + HCl -> MgCl2 + H2.::Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2||What type of reaction occurs when calcium carbonate is heated to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide?::A decomposition reaction.||State the law that requires a chemical equation to be balanced.::The law of conservation of mass, which states that matter cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Chemical reactions occur continuously around us, including the combustion (burning) of fuels and the digestion of food inside living organisms.
sla_notes_details: Combustion is an exothermic combination reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases heat and light energy, for example the burning of methane gas: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Digestion involves decomposition reactions in which large food molecules, such as starch, are broken down by enzymes into simpler, soluble molecules, such as glucose, that the body can absorb and use for energy.
sla_notes_illustrations: Complete combustion of charcoal (carbon) with plenty of oxygen produces carbon dioxide: C + O2 -> CO2, while incomplete combustion with insufficient oxygen produces poisonous carbon monoxide, CO.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding combustion helps explain why kitchens must be well ventilated when using charcoal or gas stoves, to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for the complete combustion of methane gas.::CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O||What poisonous gas can form during incomplete combustion of carbon-based fuels?::Carbon monoxide, CO.||What type of chemical process breaks down starch into glucose during digestion?::A decomposition reaction (hydrolysis) catalysed by enzymes.

learning_activity_name: Describe acids, bases and salts (reactions of acids and bases with various substances) and their applications in daily life
sla_name: Acids, Bases and Salts: Reactions and Applications
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly test and classify given substances as acids, bases or salts based on their reactions.
sla_teaching_aids: Dilute hydrochloric acid|Sodium hydroxide solution|Litmus paper|Universal indicator|Test tubes|Marble chips
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H+) in water and turns blue litmus red, while a base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions (OH-) in water and turns red litmus blue; a salt is formed when an acid reacts with a base.
sla_notes_details: Acids react with reactive metals to produce a salt and hydrogen gas, with carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas, and with bases in a neutralization reaction to produce a salt and water, for example hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
sla_notes_illustrations: When an acid reacts with a carbonate, such as 2HCl + CaCO3 -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2, the carbon dioxide gas produced can be confirmed by bubbling it through limewater, which turns milky.
sla_notes_daily_life: Antacid tablets used to relieve stomach upset work by neutralizing excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
sla_exercise: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acid?::Red.||Write the equation for the neutralization of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide.::HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O||Write the equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate.::2HCl + CaCO3 -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

learning_activity_name: Explain the changes in the physical and chemical properties of elements across and down the periodic table
sla_name: Trends in Properties Across and Down the Periodic Table
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly describe how atomic size, metallic character and reactivity change across a period and down a group.
sla_teaching_aids: Periodic table chart|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The physical and chemical properties of elements change in predictable patterns, called trends, as one moves across a period or down a group in the periodic table.
sla_notes_details: Across a period from left to right, atomic size generally decreases and elements change from strongly metallic to non-metallic character, while the number of outer-shell electrons increases from 1 to 8. Down a group, atomic size increases because more electron shells are added, and the reactivity of metals increases while the reactivity of non-metals decreases.
sla_notes_illustrations: In group I, reactivity increases down the group from lithium to potassium, while in period 3, sodium (a highly metallic, reactive metal) is followed by chlorine (a reactive non-metal) and finally argon (an unreactive noble gas).
sla_notes_daily_life: This trend explains why potassium must be stored under oil because it reacts violently even with moisture in the air, unlike the much less reactive lithium.
sla_exercise: How does atomic size change across a period from left to right?::Atomic size decreases across a period from left to right.||How does reactivity of group I metals change down the group?::Reactivity of group I metals increases down the group.||Between sodium and chlorine in period 3, which is more metallic?::Sodium is more metallic than chlorine.

learning_activity_name: Use the electronic configuration of an element to locate their positions in the periodic table
sla_name: Using Electronic Configuration to Locate Elements in the Periodic Table
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly determine the group and period of an element from its electronic arrangement.
sla_teaching_aids: Periodic table chart|Manila paper|Calculators
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The electronic arrangement of an atom is directly related to its position in the periodic table: the number of occupied shells gives the period, and the number of electrons in the outer shell gives the group.
sla_notes_details: For example, an element with electronic arrangement 2,8,2 has three occupied shells, placing it in period 3, and has 2 outer electrons, placing it in group 2. This relationship allows the likely position and chemical properties of an unfamiliar element to be predicted once its electron arrangement is known.
sla_notes_illustrations: Phosphorus has electronic arrangement 2,8,5, showing that it is in period 3 (three shells) and group 15/V (5 outer electrons).
sla_notes_daily_life: Chemists use this relationship to quickly predict how a newly identified element is likely to behave and react, saving time during laboratory analysis.
sla_exercise: An element has the electronic arrangement 2,8,2. In which period and group is it found?::It is in period 3 (three shells) and group 2/II (2 outer electrons).||How many shells does an atom with electronic arrangement 2,8,5 have, and what is its group?::It has 3 shells (period 3) and is in group 15/V (5 outer electrons) — this is phosphorus.||What determines the period of an element in the periodic table?::The number of occupied electron shells in its atom.

learning_activity_name: Prepare acid-base indicators using locally available materials
sla_name: Experiment: Preparing Acid-Base Indicators from Local Materials
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly extract a working indicator solution from local plant material and describe its colour behaviour.
sla_teaching_aids: Red hibiscus flowers or red cabbage|Mortar and pestle|Ethanol or hot water|Test tubes|Filter paper and funnel
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An acid-base indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or basic (alkaline) solution, and some effective indicators can be extracted from locally available plants.
sla_notes_details: Coloured plant materials such as red hibiscus petals, red cabbage leaves or beetroot contain natural pigments called anthocyanins that change colour with pH. The plant material is crushed and boiled in water, or soaked in ethanol, to extract the pigment, and the extract is then filtered to obtain a clear indicator solution.
sla_notes_illustrations: Red cabbage extract turns pink/red in acid and green/yellow in alkali, allowing it to be used in a similar way to litmus or universal indicator.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers and gardeners without access to laboratory chemicals can use such homemade indicators to roughly check the acidity of their soil before planting crops.
sla_exercise: Name one local plant material that can be used to prepare an acid-base indicator.::Red cabbage (or red hibiscus flowers/beetroot).||What class of natural pigment in plants is responsible for the colour change used as an indicator?::Anthocyanins.||What method is used to extract the pigment from the plant material?::Crushing/boiling the material in water (or soaking in ethanol) then filtering.

sla_name: Experiment: Testing Acidity and Alkalinity Using Local Indicators
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly classify given local substances as acidic, neutral or alkaline using the prepared indicator.
sla_teaching_aids: Prepared plant indicator|Local substances (lemon juice, soap solution, ash solution)|Test tubes|Dropper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Once an indicator has been prepared, it can be used to test whether common local substances found at home or in the environment are acidic, neutral or alkaline.
sla_notes_details: A small amount of the substance to be tested is placed in a test tube and a few drops of the prepared indicator are added; the colour observed is then compared with known colours in acid and alkali to classify the substance. This practical skill links laboratory chemistry directly to everyday materials found in the home and environment.
sla_notes_illustrations: Lemon juice turns the indicator red/pink (acidic), a solution of wood ash in water turns it green (alkaline), and pure water shows little colour change (neutral).
sla_notes_daily_life: This simple test helps determine, for example, whether soil or water in a locality is too acidic or too alkaline for growing certain crops.
sla_exercise: What colour does red cabbage extract turn in an acidic substance such as lemon juice?::Pink/red.||What colour does red cabbage extract turn in an alkaline substance such as wood ash solution?::Green.||Why is testing soil acidity useful to farmers?::It helps them determine whether the soil is suitable for the crop they intend to grow, or whether it needs treatment (e.g. liming).

learning_activity_name: Describe the mole concept (comparison of the mole with other units of measurements and molar quantities of substances)
sla_name: The Mole Concept and Molar Quantities
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly convert between mass, number of moles and number of particles for a given substance.
sla_teaching_aids: Calculators|Periodic table|Weighing balance|Molar mass reference chart
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A mole is the SI unit for the amount of substance, defined as the amount that contains the same number of particles, 6.02 x 10^23 (Avogadro's number), as there are atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12.
sla_notes_details: The mole links the microscopic world of atoms and molecules to measurable quantities in the laboratory, such as mass in grams. The number of moles of a substance is calculated as mass divided by molar mass (n = m/M), and molar volume states that one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm3 (22,400 cm3) at standard temperature and pressure (STP).
sla_notes_illustrations: The number of moles in 36 g of water (molar mass 18 g/mol) is 36 divided by 18, which equals 2 moles, containing 2 x 6.02 x 10^23 water molecules.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pharmacists use mole calculations to prepare medicines and solutions at the correct concentration for safe dosing of patients.
sla_exercise: What is Avogadro's number?::6.02 x 10^23 particles per mole.||Calculate the number of moles in 36 g of water (molar mass = 18 g/mol).::2 moles (36/18 = 2).||What volume does one mole of any gas occupy at standard temperature and pressure (STP)?::22.4 dm3 (22,400 cm3).

learning_activity_name: Explain Avogadro's law in relation to molar quantities
sla_name: Avogadro's Law and Molar Quantities of Gases
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly apply Avogadro's law to calculate the volume or number of moles of a gas.
sla_teaching_aids: Gas jars|Periodic table|Calculators|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.
sla_notes_details: This means that one mole of any gas, regardless of its identity, occupies the same volume, 22.4 dm3, at standard temperature and pressure. The law allows the volume of a gas produced or used in a reaction to be calculated directly from the mole ratio in a balanced chemical equation, without needing to know the gas's molar mass separately.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the reaction Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, one mole of zinc produces one mole of hydrogen gas, which occupies 22.4 dm3 at STP.
sla_notes_daily_life: Engineers apply Avogadro's law when designing gas cylinders and calculating the volume of gases such as oxygen or LPG needed for industrial or home use.
sla_exercise: State Avogadro's law.::Equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.||In the reaction Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, what volume of hydrogen gas is produced from 1 mole of zinc at STP?::22.4 dm3.||Does the volume occupied by one mole of a gas depend on the identity of the gas?::No, according to Avogadro's law, one mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure.

learning_activity_name: Explain the principles of volumetric analysis (preparation of standard solutions and volumetric calculations)
sla_name: Principles of Volumetric Analysis and Standard Solutions
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly prepare a standard solution of known concentration and explain the steps of a titration.
sla_teaching_aids: Volumetric flask|Burette|Pipette|Conical flask|Sodium carbonate|Distilled water|Phenolphthalein indicator
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Volumetric analysis is a quantitative method used to determine the concentration of a solution by reacting it with a solution of known concentration, called a standard solution.
sla_notes_details: A standard solution is prepared by accurately weighing a pure substance, dissolving it in distilled water, and making it up to a fixed volume in a volumetric flask. In titration, a burette is used to deliver a measured volume of one solution into a known volume of another solution in a conical flask, until the reaction is exactly complete, shown by a colour change of an indicator (the end point); the unknown concentration is then calculated using the relationship C1V1/n1 = C2V2/n2.
sla_notes_illustrations: To prepare 250 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 sodium carbonate solution, the required mass (0.1 x 0.25 x 106 = 2.65 g) is dissolved in distilled water and made up to the 250 cm3 mark in a volumetric flask.
sla_notes_daily_life: Quality control laboratories use volumetric analysis to check that the correct concentration of active ingredients is present in soft drinks and medicines before they are sold.
sla_exercise: What is a standard solution?::A solution whose exact concentration is accurately known.||Name one piece of apparatus used to accurately deliver a variable volume of solution during titration.::A burette.||What indicates the end point of a titration?::A sudden, permanent colour change of the indicator.

learning_activity_name: Describe the applications of volumetric analysis in real life and industrial settings as in soft drinks and cocktail making, medicine and in agriculture
sla_name: Applications of Volumetric Analysis in Industry and Daily Life
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly explain how volumetric analysis is applied in at least two named real-life or industrial settings.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts/pictures of industrial titration|Sample soft drink and medicine labels|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Volumetric analysis is widely applied outside the classroom wherever the exact concentration of a substance needs to be determined or carefully controlled.
sla_notes_details: In the beverage industry, titration is used to check the acid content of soft drinks and the alcohol content of fermented drinks, ensuring they meet required standards. In medicine, volumetric analysis determines the correct concentration of active drug ingredients in tablets and syrups, ensuring safe dosing. In agriculture, it is used to determine soil acidity and the concentration of nutrients in fertilizer solutions used, for example, in hydroponics.
sla_notes_illustrations: A citric acid content test in a soft drink involves titrating a sample against a standard sodium hydroxide solution, using phenolphthalein indicator, until a permanent pink colour appears.
sla_notes_daily_life: Consistent quality of packaged juices and cocktails from one bottle to the next depends directly on volumetric analysis carried out during production.
sla_exercise: Give one industrial application of volumetric analysis in the beverage industry.::Determining the acid content of soft drinks through titration.||How is volumetric analysis useful in the pharmaceutical industry?::It is used to determine the correct concentration of active ingredients in medicines to ensure safe dosing.||State one use of volumetric analysis in agriculture.::Determining soil acidity or the concentration of nutrients in fertilizer solutions.

learning_activity_name: Explore the basic tenets of ionic theory and electrolysis (ionic theory, mechanism of electrolysis and laws of electrolysis)
sla_name: Ionic Theory, Mechanism and Laws of Electrolysis
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly explain the movement of ions and predict the products formed at each electrode during electrolysis.
sla_teaching_aids: Electrolysis cell/Hoffman voltameter|Copper electrodes|Copper(II) sulphate solution|Battery/DC power source|Connecting wires
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Ionic theory states that when an ionic compound dissolves in water or is melted, it dissociates into freely moving charged particles called ions, which are able to conduct electricity.
sla_notes_details: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an ionic compound (electrolyte) by passing an electric current through it; positive ions (cations) migrate to the negative electrode (cathode), where they gain electrons in a reduction reaction, while negative ions (anions) migrate to the positive electrode (anode), where they lose electrons in an oxidation reaction. Faraday's laws of electrolysis state that the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed, and to the substance's chemical equivalent mass.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the electrolysis of copper(II) sulphate solution using copper electrodes, copper is deposited at the cathode, Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, while copper dissolves from the anode, Cu - 2e- -> Cu2+.
sla_notes_daily_life: Electroplating, which uses electrolysis to coat cheaper metal objects such as spoons with a thin layer of silver or chromium, relies directly on these principles.
sla_exercise: Where do positive ions (cations) move to during electrolysis?::To the cathode (negative electrode).||Write the half-equation for the deposition of copper at the cathode during electrolysis of copper(II) sulphate solution.::Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu||State one of Faraday's laws of electrolysis.::The mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

learning_activity_name: Describe the preparation and properties of various compounds of metals (oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, hydrogen carbonates, nitrates, chlorides and sulphates of metals)
sla_name: Preparation and Properties of Metal Compounds
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly describe the general methods for preparing oxides, hydroxides, carbonates and salts of metals.
sla_teaching_aids: Metal samples (magnesium, copper)|Dilute acids|Sodium hydroxide solution|Test tubes|Bunsen burner
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Metals form a wide range of compounds, including oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, hydrogen carbonates, nitrates, chlorides and sulphates, each prepared by characteristic general methods.
sla_notes_details: Metal oxides are commonly prepared by directly burning the metal in oxygen or by heating the corresponding carbonate or hydroxide; metal hydroxides are prepared by adding excess alkali to a solution of a metal salt to precipitate the insoluble hydroxide; soluble salts such as chlorides, nitrates and sulphates are prepared by reacting a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with the corresponding acid, followed by evaporation and crystallization.
sla_notes_illustrations: Copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to prepare copper(II) sulphate: CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O, and blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O, are obtained on crystallization.
sla_notes_daily_life: Copper(II) sulphate prepared this way is used by farmers as a fungicide to protect crops such as coffee and grapes from fungal diseases.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for the preparation of copper(II) sulphate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric acid.::CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O||Name one general method for preparing an insoluble metal hydroxide.::Adding excess sodium hydroxide (alkali) to a solution of the metal salt to precipitate the hydroxide.||What colour are the crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulphate?::Blue.

sla_name: Oxidizing and Displacement Properties of Non-metal Compounds
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly state whether a given non-metal compound acts as an oxidizing agent or shows displacement behaviour, supported by an equation.
sla_teaching_aids: Chlorine water|Potassium iodide solution|Hydrogen gas apparatus|Test tubes|Sulphur dioxide generator
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Several compounds of non-metals, such as chlorine, hydrogen, sulphur dioxide and ammonia, show characteristic oxidizing, reducing or displacement properties.
sla_notes_details: Chlorine is a strong oxidizing agent and can displace less reactive halogens from their salt solutions, for example displacing iodine from potassium iodide solution; sulphur dioxide commonly acts as a reducing agent, for example decolorizing acidified potassium permanganate solution; hydrogen can reduce hot metal oxides to the metal, showing its reducing property.
sla_notes_illustrations: Chlorine displacing iodine from potassium iodide: Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2; hydrogen reducing copper(II) oxide on heating: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O.
sla_notes_daily_life: Chlorine's strong oxidizing property is used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools by killing harmful micro-organisms.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for chlorine displacing iodine from potassium iodide solution.::Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2||Write the equation for hydrogen reducing copper(II) oxide.::CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O||Why is chlorine used to disinfect drinking water?::Because it is a strong oxidizing agent that kills harmful micro-organisms.

learning_activity_name: Perform experiments on volumetric analysis
sla_name: Experiment: Titration in Volumetric Analysis
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly carry out an acid-base titration and read the burette accurately to determine the volume at the end point.
sla_teaching_aids: Burette|Pipette|Conical flask|Standard sodium hydroxide solution|Dilute hydrochloric acid|Phenolphthalein indicator|Retort stand
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This practical activity gives learners hands-on experience of carrying out a titration to determine an unknown concentration using volumetric apparatus.
sla_notes_details: A measured volume of acid is pipetted into a conical flask together with a few drops of indicator, and the standard alkali is added slowly from the burette while swirling the flask, until the indicator just changes colour at the end point. The titration is repeated until two consistent (concordant) readings are obtained, and the average titre is used to calculate the unknown concentration.
sla_notes_illustrations: 25.0 cm3 of hydrochloric acid required 22.5 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide to reach the end point, from which the acid's concentration can be calculated using HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
sla_notes_daily_life: The precise measurement skills practiced here are the same skills used by laboratory technicians when testing water quality and food safety in real industries.
sla_exercise: Name one apparatus used to measure a fixed, accurate volume of acid before titration.::A pipette.||What is meant by a 'concordant' titre?::Two or more titration readings that agree closely (usually within 0.1 cm3 of each other).||If 25.0 cm3 of HCl required 22.5 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 NaOH to neutralize, write the balanced equation for the reaction.::HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O

learning_activity_name: Perform experiments on the applications of electrolysis in corrosion inhibition and purification of metals
sla_name: Experiment: Electrolysis in Corrosion Inhibition and Metal Purification
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly set up an electrolysis circuit and explain how it can protect a metal from corrosion or purify it.
sla_teaching_aids: Copper electrodes (impure and pure)|Copper(II) sulphate solution|DC power source|Iron nails|Zinc strip|Beakers
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Electrolysis is applied practically both to protect metals from corrosion and to purify impure metals to a high degree of purity.
sla_notes_details: In electroplating for corrosion protection, a metal object is made the cathode in an electrolytic cell so that a protective layer of a less reactive metal, such as zinc (galvanizing) or chromium, is deposited on its surface, preventing rusting. In electrolytic refining, an impure metal such as copper is made the anode and a strip of pure metal is made the cathode in a solution of the metal's salt; the impure metal dissolves at the anode and pure metal is deposited at the cathode, leaving the impurities behind as anode sludge.
sla_notes_illustrations: In copper refining, the impure copper anode dissolves according to Cu - 2e- -> Cu2+, while pure copper is deposited at the cathode according to Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
sla_notes_daily_life: Galvanized iron sheets (mabati) used for roofing are protected from rust by a zinc coating applied through an electrolytic process.
sla_exercise: What is electroplating?::A process that uses electrolysis to deposit a thin protective or decorative layer of metal onto the surface of another metal object.||In electrolytic refining of copper, which electrode is made of impure copper?::The anode.||Write the half-equation occurring at the anode during copper refining.::Cu - 2e- -> Cu2+

sla_notes_intro: Chemistry set-ups are often recorded as labelled diagrams, and simple computer drawing or diagramming software can be used to produce clear, professional sketches of them.
sla_notes_details: Learners use basic drawing tools, such as shapes, lines and text labels, available in software such as presentation or drawing programs, to represent apparatus like flasks, delivery tubes and electrodes in their correct relative positions. Digital sketches can be easily edited, resized, labelled and shared, which is an advantage over hand drawing when preparing laboratory reports.
sla_notes_illustrations: A digitally drawn set-up for electrolysis of copper(II) sulphate shows a beaker containing the solution, two labelled electrodes connected by wires to a battery symbol, with an arrow indicating the direction of current flow.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same digital sketching skills are used by engineers and technicians in industry to prepare clear process diagrams for training and documentation.
sla_exercise: State one advantage of using computer software to sketch an experimental set-up compared to drawing it by hand.::Digital sketches can be easily edited, resized and shared, and often look clearer/more professional.||Name one basic drawing tool feature used to label parts of a diagram in software.::A text-box/label tool.||Why is it important to label a diagram of an experimental set-up clearly?::So that anyone reading it can identify each piece of apparatus and understand how the experiment was set up.

sla_notes_intro: This practical activity allows learners to prepare a soluble salt of a metal using the general method of reacting an insoluble base or carbonate with excess dilute acid.
sla_notes_details: Excess copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulphuric acid until no more of the solid dissolves, shown by unreacted solid remaining at the bottom; the mixture is then filtered to remove the excess solid, and the filtrate is evaporated to concentrate it before being left to cool and crystallize, giving blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulphate.
sla_notes_illustrations: CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O; the crystals obtained are copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO4.5H2O.
sla_notes_daily_life: Metal salts prepared in a similar way, such as copper(II) sulphate, are sold commercially as fungicides and used in electroplating baths.
sla_exercise: Why is excess copper(II) oxide added to the dilute sulphuric acid during this preparation?::To ensure all the acid reacts completely, leaving only unreacted solid oxide which can be filtered off.||What process is used to remove excess unreacted copper(II) oxide from the mixture?::Filtration.||What process is used to obtain solid crystals from the filtrate?::Evaporation followed by cooling and crystallization.

sla_notes_intro: This practical activity allows learners to directly observe how gases such as chlorine, sulphur dioxide and ammonia behave as oxidizing or reducing agents, through colour changes and displacement reactions.
sla_notes_details: Adding chlorine water to potassium bromide solution causes a colour change as bromine is displaced and released; passing sulphur dioxide into orange acidified potassium dichromate solution turns it green as the dichromate is reduced, showing sulphur dioxide acting as a reducing agent. Learners record their observations and write balanced equations for each reaction observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2, in which chlorine displaces bromine and the solution turns orange-brown.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reactions mirror industrial bleaching processes, where chlorine-based compounds are used to bleach paper and textiles by oxidizing coloured impurities.
sla_exercise: What colour change is observed when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?::The solution turns orange/orange-brown as bromine is displaced and released.||What colour change occurs when sulphur dioxide is passed into acidified potassium dichromate solution?::The orange solution turns green.||Is sulphur dioxide acting as an oxidizing agent or a reducing agent in the reaction with potassium dichromate?::A reducing agent.

sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly outline and demonstrate the laboratory-scale stages of converting sulphur dioxide into sulphuric acid.
sla_teaching_aids: Sulphur|Bunsen burner|Delivery tubes|Vanadium(V) oxide catalyst (or model)|Test tubes|Water
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) is manufactured from sulphur dioxide through a sequence of oxidation reactions, a small-scale version of the industrial Contact process.
sla_notes_details: Sulphur is first burned in air or oxygen to produce sulphur dioxide: S + O2 -> SO2; the sulphur dioxide is then oxidized to sulphur trioxide in the presence of a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3; finally, sulphur trioxide is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum, which is then carefully diluted with water to produce sulphuric acid: SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4.
sla_notes_illustrations: This overall three-stage process converts elemental sulphur into commercially useful sulphuric acid used widely in industry.
sla_notes_daily_life: Sulphuric acid produced this way is a key raw material for manufacturing fertilizers, detergents and car battery acid.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for burning sulphur to form sulphur dioxide.::S + O2 -> SO2||Write the equation for the catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide.::2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3 (in the presence of a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst)||What is the final step in converting sulphur trioxide to sulphuric acid?::Sulphur trioxide is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum, which is then diluted with water: SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4.

sla_name: Extraction of Iron from Its Ore
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly describe the ore, stages and reduction reactions involved in extracting iron in a blast furnace.
sla_teaching_aids: Blast furnace diagram/chart|Sample of iron ore (haematite)|Coke and limestone samples|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Iron is extracted from its ore, mainly haematite (Fe2O3), through a reduction process carried out in a blast furnace.
sla_notes_details: The blast furnace is charged with iron ore, coke (carbon) and limestone (calcium carbonate); hot air blown in burns the coke to form carbon dioxide, which reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide, the main reducing agent: C + O2 -> CO2, then CO2 + C -> 2CO. Carbon monoxide reduces the iron ore to molten iron: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, while the limestone decomposes to form calcium oxide, which combines with sandy silica impurities to form slag that is removed separately from the molten iron.
sla_notes_illustrations: The key reduction step is Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, producing molten iron that collects at the bottom of the furnace.
sla_notes_daily_life: Iron extracted this way is processed into steel, used to make construction reinforcement bars, vehicles, machinery and household tools.
sla_exercise: Name the main ore of iron used in extraction.::Haematite (Fe2O3).||Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide in the blast furnace.::Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2||What is the role of limestone in the blast furnace?::It decomposes to form calcium oxide, which combines with silica impurities to form slag that is removed from the molten iron.

sla_teaching_aids: Notebook/project proposal form|Basic laboratory apparatus relevant to chosen topic|Reference books|Internet resources where available
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A research project allows learners to apply the scientific method to investigate a real chemistry-related problem of their own choice.
sla_notes_details: The process begins with identifying a researchable problem, for example testing which local water source is least contaminated, or comparing the effectiveness of different local materials as indicators, followed by stating a clear objective and hypothesis, planning a method, and systematically collecting and recording data. Learners must ensure their project is safe, practical with the resources available, and completed within the given time.
sla_notes_illustrations: A project comparing the acid-neutralizing ability of different antacid brands would involve titrating each antacid against a standard acid and comparing the volumes needed to neutralize it.
sla_notes_daily_life: Skills developed in project work, such as planning, data collection and evidence-based conclusions, are directly transferable to problem-solving in agriculture, health and small business settings.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in designing a research project?::Identifying a clear, researchable problem/question.||Why must a hypothesis be tested using systematic data collection?::To provide objective evidence that either supports or refutes the hypothesis, rather than relying on assumption.||Give one safety consideration to keep in mind when choosing a chemistry project topic.::The project should use apparatus and chemicals that are safe and available at the school.

sla_name: Basic Tenets of Qualitative Analysis
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly carry out preliminary, solution and confirmatory tests to identify an unknown ion.
sla_teaching_aids: Unknown salt samples|Dilute nitric acid|Silver nitrate solution|Sodium hydroxide solution|Test tubes|Bunsen burner
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Qualitative analysis is a systematic procedure used to identify the ions or radicals present in an unknown substance, rather than measuring how much of them is present.
sla_notes_details: Preliminary tests examine physical characteristics such as colour, smell and solubility of the sample; tests in solution involve dissolving the sample and adding reagents such as sodium hydroxide or ammonia to observe precipitate formation and colour, which suggest a possible metal ion; confirmatory tests then use a more specific, selective reagent to conclusively confirm the identity of the suspected ion.
sla_notes_illustrations: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution containing Cu2+ ions produces a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide: Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2, confirming the presence of copper(II) ions.
sla_notes_daily_life: Qualitative analysis techniques are used in forensic laboratories and hospitals to identify unknown substances, such as poisons or contaminants, from samples.
sla_exercise: What are the three main stages of qualitative analysis?::Preliminary tests, tests in solution, and confirmatory tests.||Write the equation for the reaction of copper(II) ions with sodium hydroxide.::Cu2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2||What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing Cu2+ ions?::A blue precipitate.

sla_teaching_aids: Molecular model kits|Samples of candle wax, petrol (in sealed container)|Charts of homologous series|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Organic chemistry is the study of compounds of carbon, most of which also contain hydrogen and are called hydrocarbons, together with related compounds such as alcohols.
sla_notes_details: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are open-chain compounds of carbon and hydrogen, grouped into homologous series such as alkanes (single bonds only, general formula CnH2n+2), alkenes (containing one double bond, CnH2n) and alkynes (containing one triple bond, CnH2n-2). Alcohols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl (-OH) functional group attached to a carbon chain, with the general formula CnH2n+1OH for saturated alcohols.
sla_notes_illustrations: Methane (CH4) is the simplest alkane, ethene (C2H4) is the simplest alkene, and ethanol (C2H5OH) is the alcohol found in alcoholic beverages.
sla_notes_daily_life: Methane in biogas is used as a cooking fuel in rural households, while ethanol is used both as a fuel additive and as the alcohol in fermented drinks.
sla_exercise: What is the general formula for alkanes?::CnH2n+2||What functional group is present in alcohols?::The hydroxyl group, -OH.||Name the simplest alkane and give its molecular formula.::Methane, CH4.

sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Structural formulae show how atoms are connected within an organic molecule, and computer software can be used to draw these structures quickly and accurately.
sla_notes_details: Chemistry drawing software allows learners to place carbon and hydrogen atoms, bonds and functional groups such as -OH to build correct structures for straight-chain hydrocarbons and alcohols from one to ten carbon atoms, always checking that each carbon atom forms exactly four bonds. This builds a visual understanding of chain length, branching and functional groups before formal IUPAC naming is applied.
sla_notes_illustrations: Propan-1-ol (C3H7OH) is drawn as a three-carbon chain with an -OH group attached to the end (first) carbon atom.
sla_notes_daily_life: Chemical structure drawing software of this kind is used by pharmaceutical and food companies to design and communicate the structures of new compounds.
sla_exercise: What must be true about the number of bonds formed by every carbon atom in an organic structure?::Every carbon atom must form exactly four bonds.||On which carbon atom is the -OH group attached in propan-1-ol?::The first (end) carbon atom.||State one benefit of using structure-drawing software when learning organic chemistry.::It helps learners visualize chain length, branching and functional groups accurately and quickly.

sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly assign IUPAC names to given straight-chain hydrocarbons and alcohols with up to ten carbon atoms.
sla_teaching_aids: IUPAC naming chart (prefixes meth- to dec-)|Chemistry naming software|Molecular models|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The IUPAC system provides standard rules for naming organic compounds, based on the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain and the functional group present.
sla_notes_details: The root of the name is based on the number of carbon atoms present (meth- for 1, eth- for 2, prop- for 3, but- for 4, pent- for 5, hex- for 6, hept- for 7, oct- for 8, non- for 9, dec- for 10), combined with a suffix that shows the type of compound: '-ane' for alkanes, '-ene' for alkenes, and '-ol' for alcohols, with a locant number showing the position of any double bond or -OH group where needed.
sla_notes_illustrations: A five-carbon alkane is named pentane (C5H12), while a four-carbon alcohol with the -OH group on the second carbon is named butan-2-ol.
sla_notes_daily_life: Correctly naming compounds using the IUPAC system ensures that chemists, doctors and industries anywhere in the world understand exactly which compound is being referred to, preventing dangerous mix-ups.
sla_exercise: What prefix is used in IUPAC names for a five-carbon chain?::Pent-||Name the compound C5H12 using the IUPAC system.::Pentane.||What suffix is used in the IUPAC name of an alcohol?::-ol

sla_name: Chemical Reactions of Aliphatic Hydrocarbons and Alcohols
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly predict and write equations for the typical reactions of a given hydrocarbon or alcohol based on its structure.
sla_teaching_aids: Ethene gas (or model)|Bromine water|Ethanol|Sodium metal (small piece)|Test tubes|Bunsen burner
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The chemical reactions of aliphatic hydrocarbons and alcohols are determined by their structure, particularly whether they contain only single bonds, a double bond, or the hydroxyl functional group.
sla_notes_details: Alkanes, having only single bonds, are generally unreactive except for combustion and substitution reactions with halogens under sunlight; alkenes, having a reactive double bond, readily undergo addition reactions, such as decolorizing orange bromine water; alcohols, due to their reactive -OH group, undergo combustion, react with reactive metals such as sodium to release hydrogen gas, and can be oxidized to form carboxylic acids.
sla_notes_illustrations: Ethene reacting with bromine water: C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2, the decolorization confirming a double bond is present; ethanol reacting with sodium: 2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2.
sla_notes_daily_life: The bromine water test taught here is the same simple test used to check whether cooking oils are saturated or unsaturated (and therefore healthier), based on how quickly the orange colour disappears.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for ethene reacting with bromine water.::C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2||Why do alkenes react more readily than alkanes?::Because alkenes have a reactive carbon-carbon double bond that readily undergoes addition reactions, unlike the single bonds in alkanes.||Write the equation for ethanol reacting with sodium metal.::2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2

sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly follow the systematic procedure to identify the cation and anion present in an unknown sample.
sla_teaching_aids: Unknown salt sample|Sodium hydroxide solution|Ammonia solution|Barium chloride solution|Dilute hydrochloric acid|Test tubes
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This practical activity requires learners to apply the systematic steps of qualitative analysis to identify an unknown chemical substance provided in the laboratory.
sla_notes_details: Learners first record preliminary observations, such as colour and solubility, then carry out solution tests by adding sodium hydroxide and ammonia dropwise and in excess, observing any precipitate colour and whether it dissolves in excess reagent, before applying confirmatory tests specific to the suspected ion to reach a final identification, recording all findings in a results table.
sla_notes_illustrations: A white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide but not in excess ammonia indicates the presence of Al3+ or Pb2+ ions, which are then distinguished further using specific confirmatory tests.
sla_notes_daily_life: The disciplined, step-by-step method practiced here mirrors procedures followed by water quality technicians who identify contaminants in community water sources.
sla_exercise: What observation suggests the presence of Al3+ or Pb2+ ions when testing with sodium hydroxide?::A white precipitate forms that dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide is added.||Why is the test repeated with ammonia solution in addition to sodium hydroxide?::Because different metal ions behave differently with the two reagents, helping to distinguish between similar-looking precipitates.||Why must all observations be recorded in a results table during qualitative analysis?::To keep an organized, reliable record that supports accurate identification of the unknown ions.

sla_name: Local and Industrial Preparation of Hydrocarbons and Alcohols
sla_assessment_criteria: Learners correctly describe and, where possible, demonstrate a local or industrial method for preparing a named hydrocarbon or alcohol.
sla_teaching_aids: Fermentation set-up (yeast, sugar solution, flask, delivery tube)|Limewater|Distillation apparatus|Molasses sample
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Hydrocarbons and alcohols can be obtained through both traditional local methods and large-scale industrial processes.
sla_notes_details: Ethanol is traditionally prepared locally by fermentation, in which yeast enzymes convert sugars from materials such as molasses or ripe fruit into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, followed by distillation to concentrate and purify the alcohol. Industrially, ethanol can also be produced by the catalytic hydration of ethene gas obtained from the cracking of petroleum, while hydrocarbons such as petrol and diesel are obtained industrially through fractional distillation of crude oil.
sla_notes_illustrations: Fermentation of molasses produces ethanol used in local drinks and industrially, and the carbon dioxide released during fermentation can be confirmed by passing it through limewater, which turns milky.
sla_notes_daily_life: Locally fermented and distilled ethanol is used both in traditional beverages and, increasingly, as a biofuel blended with petrol to reduce fuel costs and pollution.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for the fermentation of glucose to produce ethanol.::C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2||What process is used to purify and concentrate ethanol after fermentation?::Distillation.||How is the carbon dioxide produced during fermentation confirmed?::By passing the gas through limewater, which turns milky.

sla_notes_intro: This activity concludes the research project started in Form Three by requiring learners to analyse their collected data and compile a complete written scientific report.
sla_notes_details: A complete project report includes a title, an introduction/objective, materials and method, results (often presented in tables and graphs), a discussion of findings, a conclusion, and references; learners must ensure their conclusions are properly supported by the data they collected and that any chemical equations or calculations used are accurate. The final report is submitted for assessment following the school's or examination body's required format.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a project on titrating different antacid brands, the report would present a table and a bar graph comparing the volume of acid neutralized by each brand, with a conclusion identifying the most effective brand supported by the data.
sla_notes_daily_life: The report-writing skills developed here mirror those needed in real scientific, agricultural and industrial careers, where findings must be clearly documented and communicated to others.
sla_exercise: Name three sections that should be included in a chemistry project report.::Introduction/objective, materials and method, and results (also discussion, conclusion, references).||Why must the conclusion of a project report be supported by the data collected?::Because scientific conclusions must be based on objective evidence, not opinion, to be credible and valid.||Give one way results can be presented clearly in a project report.::Using tables and graphs to summarize and visualize the data.
